# Motion

> Generates a set of motion tokens for a design system: named easings — cubic-bezier
> or spring — each with its own duration, a derived and deliberately faster exit, a
> per-motion stagger, and purpose aliases that map components onto them. Exports to
> CSS, Tailwind v4, Framer Motion and DTCG, with the cost of each conversion measured
> rather than hidden.

Free, no account, no API key, no rate limit. Every set is a pure function of the URL,
so the same link always returns the same tokens.

Site: https://www.springs.studio

## Using this as a tool

Fetch the page. The motion set is in the HTML — no JavaScript required.

  https://www.springs.studio/

Two readable blocks sit at the end of the document:

  <script type="application/json" id="motion-studio-tokens">  structured data
  <pre>                                                       the same set as text

For JSON alone, swap the path:

  https://www.springs.studio/api/tokens

Both accept the same query string, so a share link works on either.

The ready-made CSS, Tailwind theme, Framer Motion transitions and DTCG file are
in that JSON under `formats`. They are deliberately not in the page text: if
you are reading the page as markdown, the JSON was stripped along with the
script tag holding it, so fetch /api/tokens rather than rebuilding a stylesheet
from the token table.

## Query contract

Every parameter is optional. With none, you get the shipped default set.

  e    Repeated once per motion. Six fields, separated by "*":
         id*name*easing*durationMs*exit*staggerMs
       easing is either
         b.<x1>.<y1>.<x2>.<y2>
           cubic-bezier. All four values are multiplied by 100, so
           cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) is written b.20.0.0.100
         s.<stiffness>.<damping>.<mass>.<velocity>
           spring. stiffness and damping are written as-is; mass and velocity
           are multiplied by 100, so stiffness 400, damping 12, mass 1 is
           written s.400.12.100.0
       exit is either
         r<percent>   a share of the entrance, e.g. r70
         a<ms>        an absolute duration, e.g. a140
  pu   One value, not repeated: the entry id for each purpose in the order
       below, joined by ".", e.g. pu=sub.std.std.std.emp.emp.emp
  xt   Tokens held out of the export: <entryId>*<enter|exit>, "." between
       entries, e.g. xt=sub*exit.emp*enter
  tol  Spring sampling tolerance for the CSS linear() approximation, in
       ten-thousandths, 1-2000. Default 100, i.e. 1%. The UI offers 300 (3%),
       100 (1%) and 30 (0.3%).

Purposes, in the order `pu` expects them:
  state, dropdown, tooltip, list, drawer, modal, toast

A complete example — one bouncy spring named "pop", 300ms, exit at 70% of the
entrance, 40ms stagger, used by every purpose:

  https://www.springs.studio/?e=pop*pop*s.400.12.100.0*300*r70*40&pu=pop.pop.pop.pop.pop.pop.pop

## What comes back

Each motion publishes two tokens:

  motion.<slug>.enter
  motion.<slug>.exit

and each purpose aliases one of them:

  motion.<purpose>-enter -> var(--motion-<slug>-enter)

## When a link arrives incomplete

Some fetchers keep only the first of a repeated query key, which would leave one
`e` and a `pu` pointing at motions that are no longer present. Rather than
quietly repointing them, the response carries a `warnings` array and the page
text opens with "This link did not arrive intact", naming the missing ids and
how many motions the original had. If you see it, re-fetch preserving every
repeated `e` before drawing any conclusion about the set.

## Stability

The JSON at /api/tokens carries a `version` integer, currently 1.

Keys are only ever added. An existing key will not be removed, retyped, or
given a new meaning without `version` changing — so parse defensively for keys
you do not recognise, and treat a `version` you do not know as a reason to stop
rather than to guess.

## Rules that matter when applying these

- Entrances decelerate: fast at the start, settling into rest. An entrance that
  accelerates into its resting place is the most common way a set feels wrong,
  and neither the durations nor the stagger will reveal it. Every token reports
  a `direction` of decelerating, accelerating or linear, so this is checkable.
- Prefer the purpose aliases or the named motions over raw durations.
- Exits stay faster and flatter than entrances. That asymmetry is deliberate;
  symmetric motion reads as sluggish on the way out.
- Ship the prefers-reduced-motion block. It is already in the CSS export.
- A spring has no duration. `durationMs` on a spring token is the window Framer
  Motion plays, and the CSS `linear()` is sampled across it, so it must not be
  shortened — but it overstates when the motion is perceptually over. Spring
  tokens carry `settlesMs` beside it — within 1% of target, whatever the
  velocity at that moment — which is the number to compare against a bezier's
  duration. A settling estimate, not a fact — copying it onto a CSS transition will not reproduce the
  motion. Use the sampled `linear()` in the token's `css` field, or the spring
  parameters with a runtime that does real physics.
- CSS cannot run spring physics, so springs are sampled into a `linear()`
  polyline. `conversionCost.css` in the JSON reports the worst-case error across
  the set, measured against the exact closed-form curve.
- DTCG has no spring type. `$value` carries a linear fallback and the real
  parameters travel in `$extensions["studio.motion.spring"]`.
